result: The authors propose a new disposition mechanism called Hepatoenteric Recycling (HER), where the intestine is the metabolic organ for glucuronide formation and the liver is the recycling organ. This mechanism is distinct from classical enterohepatic recycling (EHR) where the liver forms metabolites and the intestine recycles them. The authors demonstrate that certain glucuronides are efficiently recycled by the liver via OATP1B1/1B3/2B1 transporters, and that hepatic uptake is the rate-limiting step.
evaluation: Claims C2-C6, C17, and C63 collectively establish the HER mechanism through multiple lines of evidence: portal vein infusion experiments showing efficient hepatic recycling of glucuronides (C2), identification of OATP transporters as responsible for uptake (C3), demonstration that hepatic uptake is rate-limiting (C4), intestinal perfusion studies showing intestinal glucuronidation (C5), and clear definition distinguishing HER from EHR (C6, C17, C63). The experimental data from Figures 1-6 and Table 1 provide converging support for this novel mechanism.

result: Portal vein infusion of Won-7-G at various concentrations (2-1000 μM) showed that biliary secretion and blood concentrations reached steady state after 1 hour. LRE% decreased significantly at higher concentrations, and biliary excretion rates showed saturation kinetics at blood concentrations ≥100 μM, indicating transporter-mediated excretion.
evaluation: Claims C20-C24 describe concentration-dependent effects on Won-7-G recycling with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.05) and are supported by data in Figure 2A1-A4. The saturation kinetics at higher concentrations provide evidence for transporter-mediated processes, consistent with the proposed mechanism.

result: All seven glucuronides tested showed significantly higher LRE% than their corresponding aglycones (p<0.05). Wogonin had the highest LRE% (41%) among aglycones when recycled as Won-7-G, while other aglycones showed <10% LRE%. The lower LRE% of aglycones was attributed to slow hepatic metabolism rather than uptake limitations or protein binding.
evaluation: Claims C25-C31 are well-supported by experimental data in Table 1 and Figure 2B1-B7, with appropriate statistical analysis. The mechanistic explanation for lower aglycone LRE% is supported by uptake studies (C28), concentration experiments ruling out protein binding effects (C29), and liver tissue concentration measurements (C30). The interpretation that slow hepatic metabolism limits aglycone LRE% (C31) is a reasonable inference from the data.

result: LRE% of 16 phenolic-O-glucuronides varied widely (5-95%), and glucuronidation at the 7-position alone was insufficient to predict high LRE%, indicating that aglycone structure is an important determinant. Sex differences were minimal for Won-7-G and Lut-3'-G, but Bai-7-G showed increased LRE% in female rats (p<0.05).
evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by experimental data from testing 16 glucuronides (Appendix 2—table 5) and sex comparison studies (Appendix 2—table 6). The structure-activity relationship conclusion (C33) is appropriately cautious, acknowledging that position of glucuronidation alone doesn't determine LRE%. The sex difference findings are statistically supported.

result: Cassette dosing of multiple glucuronides at low concentration (10 μM) did not significantly impact LRE%, indicating the hepatic recycling system can handle multiple glucuronides simultaneously at this concentration.
evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D showing no significant differences between single and cassette dosing. This is a useful methodological finding that enables efficient screening of multiple compounds.

result: Uptake of glucuronides by OATP1B1/1B3/2B1-expressing cells varied significantly between glucuronides and between transporters (p<0.005). Most glucuronides with high LRE% showed rapid uptake in OATP cells, with Km values in the micromolar range. Lut-3'-G showed an exception due to further metabolism to di-glucuronides in liver.
evaluation: Claims C37-C42 are supported by cellular uptake data in Figure 3A-B and kinetic parameters in Appendix 2—table 7. The explanation for Lut-3'-G discrepancy (C40-C41) is supported by both literature citation and experimental LC-MS confirmation in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, demonstrating thorough investigation of an apparent exception to the general pattern.

result: Rifampicin (25 μM) potently inhibited (>90%) uptake of OATP1B1/1B3 substrates, while telmisartan inhibited OATP2B1 substrates. Cross-inhibition studies showed that non-inhibitors of prototypical OATP substrates were not substrates themselves, but OATP substrates could inhibit uptake of glucuronides. Interestingly, aglycones were better inhibitors than their glucuronides despite lower LRE%.
evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by inhibition data in Figure 3C1-C3 and cross-inhibition studies in Figure 3D1-D3. The findings are internally consistent and supported by literature (C44). The observation that aglycones are better inhibitors than glucuronides (C48) is interesting and well-documented, though the mechanistic explanation would require further investigation.

result: Statistical analysis using Fisher exact test showed 93.2% (41/44) of combinations demonstrated significant correlation between cellular uptake and LRE%, establishing that cellular uptake of glucuronides is the rate-limiting step in HER. This correlation was mathematically described by an Emax model (Emax 86±17%, EC50 42±33 nM).
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by comprehensive statistical analysis (Appendix 4—tables 1-2) and mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4. The high percentage of significant correlations (93.2%) provides strong evidence for the rate-limiting role of hepatic uptake. The Emax model provides a quantitative framework for understanding the relationship, though the large standard error on EC50 (±33 nM) suggests some uncertainty in this parameter.

result: Compounds with higher LRE% displayed longer elimination half-lives, and double peaks were observed in plasma profiles of orally administered phenolics with high LRE% (wogonin, ezetimibe), consistent with the HER mechanism prolonging exposure.
evaluation: Claims C52, C67-C68 are supported by pharmacokinetic data in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 3. The correlation between LRE% and half-life is expected and provides validation of the HER concept's pharmacokinetic implications. The double-peak phenomenon is characteristic of recycling processes and provides additional evidence for HER.

result: Intestinal perfusion studies showed that biliary excretion rates of five phenolic glucuronides were similar when aglycones were perfused through the intestine versus when glucuronides were infused directly into the portal vein, and significantly higher than with direct hepatic infusion of aglycones (except raloxifene). Portal vein glucuronide concentrations were significantly higher than tail vein (p<0.01), indicating the intestine serves as the major metabolic organ.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by intestinal perfusion data in Table 1 and Figure 5. These experiments provide critical evidence that intestinal metabolism is the primary source of glucuronides entering the liver, supporting the HER mechanism. The exception for raloxifene (C57) is appropriately explained by its dual metabolism in both liver and intestine.

result: OATP inhibitors (rifampicin, telmisartan, E2G, E1S at 1 mM) decreased Won-7-G LRE% from ~80% to ~40% and Lut-3'-G LRE% from ~7% to ~3%, demonstrating that OATPs play a major role in hepatic recycling. However, incomplete inhibition suggests other uptake transporters may also participate.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by in vivo inhibition data in Figure 6A-D. The substantial but incomplete inhibition of LRE% by OATP inhibitors provides strong evidence for OATP involvement while appropriately acknowledging that other transporters may contribute. The interpretation is cautious and scientifically sound.

result: Won-7-G, Api-7-G, and Bai-7-G remained >80% stable in blood for 2.5 hours at concentrations of 2, 10, and 25 μM, confirming that the glucuronides are stable during the experimental timeframe.
evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by stability data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. This is an important control experiment that validates the experimental approach by confirming that observed changes in glucuronide concentrations are due to biological processes rather than chemical degradation.

result: Multiple lines of evidence support HER for wogonin and ezetimibe: (1) high LRE% when glucuronides were infused into portal vein, (2) portal vein glucuronide concentrations much higher than aglycones in intestinal perfusion, (3) direct aglycone infusion less effective than glucuronide infusion for biliary excretion, (4) saturable OATP-mediated uptake, and (5) substantial structural impact on LRE%. These findings establish that intestine is the glucuronide-forming organ and liver is the recycling organ.
evaluation: Claims C84-C89 synthesize multiple experimental findings (from Figures 2-5, Table 1, Appendix 2—table 5) to support the HER mechanism for specific compounds. The convergence of evidence from different experimental approaches (portal vein infusion, intestinal perfusion, cellular uptake, inhibition studies) provides strong support for the conclusion that HER properly describes the disposition of these compounds.

result: HER differs from EHR in that hepatic OATPs (not intestinal transporters like ASBT) are rate-limiting, and hepatic transporters determine plasma glucuronide concentrations more than hepatic enzymes. For extrahepatically generated glucuronides, HER is critically important because glucuronides are more efficiently excreted into bile than aglycones, making HER more important than EHR for phenolics with rapid intestinal glucuronidation.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C69-C70 present key mechanistic distinctions between HER and EHR, supported by the collective experimental evidence. The conclusion that transporters are more important than enzymes in determining glucuronide disposition (C66) is a significant insight supported by the data. The claim that HER is more important than EHR for rapidly intestinally-metabolized phenolics (C70) is well-supported by the intestinal perfusion data showing >80% intestinal metabolism.

result: The HER mechanism can explain the pharmacokinetic behaviors of phenolic drugs including ezetimibe, raloxifene, and diclofenac, which show rapid intestinal glucuronidation and double-peak PK profiles. For compounds with extensive intestinal glucuronidation and hepatic recycling, HER fully explains their pharmacokinetic behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C91-C96 extend the HER concept to other drugs based on literature data (C92, C94-C95) and the authors' experimental findings. The interpretation is appropriately supported by citations showing these drugs undergo extensive intestinal glucuronidation (>80-95%) and exhibit double-peak profiles characteristic of recycling. The conclusion (C96) is reasonable but somewhat overstated—'fully explain' may be too strong given the complexity of drug disposition.

result: Some glucuronides (Lut-G, Ica-G) showed discrepancies between OATP uptake and LRE% because they undergo further hepatic metabolism to di-glucuronides. Maximum 50% inhibition of LRE% by OATP inhibitors suggests other transporters (possibly OAT3 subfamily) may contribute. Good OATP uptake correlates with high LRE% when glucuronides are not further metabolized.
evaluation: Claims C97-C100 address exceptions and limitations of the model. C97 is supported by experimental data showing di-glucuronide formation. C98 is supported by Figure 6 data. C99 is appropriately presented as speculation based on literature evidence. C100 provides a refined understanding of when OATP uptake predicts LRE%, acknowledging the importance of subsequent metabolism.

result: HER has important implications for drug disposition and drug-drug interactions. It shuttles phenolic compounds to the colon where they can have beneficial or toxic effects. The HER concept helps explain why hepatic UGT inhibitors don't always affect plasma concentrations as expected, and why OATP inhibitors can increase both aglycone and glucuronide concentrations. Pathological conditions affecting intestinal UGTs or hepatic OATPs will significantly impact disposition of phenolics undergoing HER.
evaluation: Claims C73-C83 present important implications and interpretations of HER, but most are speculative or based on inference rather than direct experimental evidence from this study. While the reasoning is logical and supported by literature citations (C71-C72, C75, C81), these claims represent predictions and hypotheses about HER's impact rather than demonstrated results. The implications are plausible but would require additional experimental validation.

result: HER potential can be readily estimated using OATP-overexpressing cells and confirmed using portal vein perfusion, which is convenient for cassette dosing. This approach could enable medicinal chemists to design compounds with intestinal glucuronidation tailored to treat intestinal diseases.
evaluation: Claim C101 is supported by the demonstrated correlation between cellular uptake and LRE% (C49-C51) and the validation of cassette dosing (C36). This represents a practical methodological contribution. Claim C102 is more speculative about future applications but is a reasonable extension of the findings.

result: The authors propose HER as a new disposition terminology to describe phenolic drugs and phytochemicals taken orally where the intestine is the major metabolism organ and liver is the recycling organ. This terminology more accurately captures the recycling of these compounds compared to EHR, and may help predict drug-drug interactions and delineate mechanisms involving intestinal UGTs and hepatic transporters.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 summarize the main conclusion of the study, which is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence. The proposal of new terminology is justified by the mechanistic distinctions demonstrated. Claims C105-C106 about future utility are more speculative but represent reasonable predictions based on the established mechanism.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on enterohepatic recycling (EHR), its historical development, importance for endogenous and exogenous compounds, and prior observations that certain intestinally-formed glucuronides can be taken up by hepatocytes. The authors note that disposition of phase II metabolites can change with age, gender, and disease conditions.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C19, C64, C71-C72, C74-C75, C90 represent background knowledge and prior work that contextualizes the current study. These are appropriately cited and provide the foundation for proposing the HER mechanism. While these are not novel findings from this study, they are accurately presented and properly attributed.
